In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta. Sin. Mim.﴾

﴿These are the verses of the clear Book.﴾

﴿We recite to you﴾: We read it with the recitation of Jibril (Gabriel). It is also permissible that it means "We send it down," used figuratively. ﴿Some of the news of Musa and Fir'awn﴾: "some of their news" is the object of ﴿نَتْلُو﴾ (natlu, "We recite"). ﴿With truth﴾: being truthful. ﴿For a people who believe﴾: because they are the ones who benefit from it.

﴿Indeed, Fir'awn exalted himself in the land﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) that explains that part of the news. The land is the land of Egypt. ﴿And made its people into factions (شِيَعًا, shiya')﴾: groups who follow him in what he wants, or who support one another in obeying him; or categories, employing each category in a particular task; or parties, by stirring up enmity among them so that they would not unite against him. ﴿Subjugating a group of them﴾: they are the Children of Israel. This clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of ﴿جَعَلَ﴾ (ja'ala, "made"), or an attributive description of ﴿شِيَعًا﴾, or a resumptive sentence. His words ﴿slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive﴾ are an apposition (badal) to it. That was because a soothsayer told him that a boy would be born among the Children of Israel through whom his kingdom would be lost. This was of the utmost foolishness: if the prediction was true, killing would not prevent it, and if it was false, then what is its basis? ﴿Indeed he was among the corrupters﴾: therefore he dared to kill a great many children of the prophets, on account of a corrupt imagining.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 7–8:

﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa﴾ by inspiration (ilham) or by a dream. ﴿Suckle him﴾ for as long as you are able to conceal him. ﴿And when you fear for him﴾ that he might be perceived. ﴿Then cast him into the sea﴾ into the sea (al-bahr), meaning the Nile. ﴿And do not fear﴾ for him any loss or harm, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ over his separation from you.

﴿Indeed, We will return him to you﴾ soon, such that you will be safe with regard to him. ﴿And We will make him one of the messengers﴾. It is narrated that when the birth pangs seized her, she summoned a midwife from those appointed over the pregnant women of the Children of Israel, and she attended to her. When Musa fell onto the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, her joints trembled, and love for him entered her heart to the extent that it prevented her from informing on him. So she nursed him for three months. Then Pharaoh pressed hard in seeking the newborn boys, and the spies strove to search for them, so she took for him a chest (tabut) and cast him into the Nile.

﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾. This is a statement of the reason for their taking him up, namely its outcome and consequence, likening it to the purpose that prompted it. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-huznan﴾ (with a sukun on the ha'). ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh, Haman and their hosts were ever sinning﴾ in everything. Therefore it is no wonder that they killed thousands on his account and then took him to raise him, so that he would grow up and do to them what they feared. Or they were wrongdoers, and God the Exalted punished them by having My Lord make their enemy at their own hands. Thus the clause is a parenthetical insertion to emphasize their error, or to explain the cause of what they were afflicted with. It was also read as ﴿khatin﴾, a lightened form of ﴿khati'in﴾, or ﴿khatin﴾ meaning those who turn the right into the wrong.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 10–11:

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became empty﴾, emptied of reason, because of the fear and bewilderment that overwhelmed her when she heard that he had fallen into the hand of Pharaoh. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their hearts are void﴾, that is, hollow, with no understanding in them. It is supported by the reading "faragan" (فَرَغًا), from their saying "dimā'uhum baynahum faragun" (دِماؤُهم بَيْنَهم فَرَغٌ), meaning wasted, i.e., shed without retribution. Or it is from grief (al-hamm), because of the intensity of her confidence in God's promise, or because she heard that Pharaoh had shown kindness to him and adopted him. ﴿Had she not been that she would have disclosed him﴾, that she was about to reveal Moses, that is, his matter and his story, out of the excess of her distress or of joy at his adoption.

﴿Had We not bound fast her heart﴾ with patience and steadfastness, ﴿that she might be among the believers﴾, among those who affirmed God's promise, or among those who were confident in His preservation of him, not in Pharaoh's adoption and kindness. It is also read "Mu'sa" (مُؤْسى), applying the dammah in the vicinity of the waw the same treatment as its dammah in the case of demanding that its hamza be a waw-hamza, as in "wujūh" (وُجُوهٌ). This is the cause of the binding. The answer to "lawla" (لَوْلا) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it.

﴿And she said to his sister﴾, Maryam. ﴿Follow him up﴾, follow his trace and pursue his news. ﴿So she watched him from afar﴾, from a distance. It is also read "'an jānib" (عَنْ جانِبٍ) and "'an janb" (عَنْ جَنْبٍ), and it has the same meaning. ﴿While they did not perceive﴾, that she was following him up, or that she was his sister.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 12–13:

﴿And We forbade him the wet-nurses﴾: We prevented him from suckling from the nursing women. It is the plural of *murdi'* or *murda'* (a nurse), and it is also the act of nursing (*ar-ridā'*), or its place, meaning the breast. ﴿Before that﴾: before the sister's tracking of him. ﴿Then she said, "Shall I direct you to a household who will nurse him for you?"﴾ on your behalf. ﴿And they will be sincere to him﴾: they will not fall short in his nursing and rearing.

It is narrated that when Haman heard this, he said: "She knows him and his family, so seize her until she tells of his condition." She said: "I only meant that they are sincere to the king." So Pharaoh ordered her to bring someone who would nurse him, and she brought his mother. Moses was on Pharaoh's lap, crying, and Pharaoh was trying to soothe him. When he smelled her scent, he was comforted and took her breast into his mouth. Pharaoh said to her, "Who are you to him? He has refused every breast except yours." She said: "I am a woman of good scent and good milk; no infant is brought to me but that he accepts me." So he gave the child to her and assigned her a stipend, and she returned with him to her house that same day. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be cooled﴾ by her child. ﴿And that she would not grieve﴾ over his separation. ﴿And that she might know that the promise of Allah is true﴾ with *'ilm mushāhada* (knowledge by direct witnessing).

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that His promise is true, so they doubt it. Or, the primary purpose of the return was her knowledge of this, and everything else is secondary. In it there is an allusion to what had escaped from her when she heard of his falling into Pharaoh's hand.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 14–15:**

﴿And when he reached his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾, meaning the stage beyond which his growth does not increase, and this is from thirty to forty years, for then the intellect (ʿaql) reaches completion.

It is narrated that "no prophet was sent except at the age of forty years."

﴿And he became perfect (istawa)﴾, meaning his physical build or his intellect. ﴿We gave him judgment (hukman)﴾, meaning prophethood (nubuwwa). ﴿And knowledge (ʿilman)﴾ of the religion, or the knowledge and bearing of the wise and the scholars before his prophetic commission, so that he would not say or do anything for which he would be considered ignorant. This reading is more consistent with the arrangement of the narrative, since the prophetic commission came after the migration, in the context of the back-and-forth. ﴿And thus﴾, that is, in the same way as what We did with Musa and his mother. ﴿We reward the doers of good﴾ for their good deeds.

﴿And he entered the city (al-madina)﴾, meaning he entered Egypt, coming from the palace of Pharaoh. It is said it was Memphis (Manf), or Haʾin, or ʿAyn Shams, from its outskirts.

﴿At a time of unawareness on the part of its people﴾, at a time when he did not habitually enter it and they did not expect him. It is said it was the time of the midday rest, and it is said it was between the two evening prayers (al-ʿishaʾayn). ﴿He found in it two men fighting, one from his own party and the other from his enemies﴾. One of them was among those who followed him in his religion, namely the Children of Israel, and the other was among his opponents, namely the Copts. The demonstrative is used as a narrative reference. ﴿So the one from his party sought his aid against the one who was﴾ ﴿from his enemies﴾, meaning he asked him to help him by lending support. For this reason the verb was construed with ﴿عَلى﴾ (ʿalā, "against"). It was also recited as ﴿اسْتَعانَهُ﴾ (istaʿānahu, "sought his help").

﴿So Musa struck him (fawakazahu)﴾, meaning he struck the Copt with the flat of his hand, and it was recited as ﴿فَلَكَزَهُ﴾ (falakazahu), meaning he struck him on the chest with it. ﴿Then he put an end to him (faqadā ʿalayhi)﴾, meaning he killed him. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 20–22:

﴿And a man came running from the farthest part of the city.﴾ Yas'a (running) is a qualifier of "a man," or a circumstantial state (hal) from him, if "from the farthest part of the city" is made a qualifier of him rather than a complement of "came," because specifying him with it links him to the definite (ma'arif).

﴿He said, "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you."﴾ Ya'tamirun means they are consulting on account of you. The consultation is called i'timar because each of the consulting parties commands the other and is commanded by him.

﴿So leave; indeed I am to you among the sincere advisers.﴾ The lam is for clarification (li'l-bayan) and is not a complement of "the sincere advisers" (al-nasihin), because the complement of a relative clause (silah) cannot precede the relative pronoun.

﴿So he left it, fearful, watching out.﴾ From the city. Fearful, watching out for the pursuit of a seeker. ﴿He said, "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people."﴾ Rescue me from them and protect me from their pursuit.

﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾ opposite Madyan, the town of Shu'ayb, named after Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them, and it was not under the rule of Pharaoh, and the distance between it and Egypt was eight (days' journey). ﴿He said, "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right way."﴾ Out of reliance upon God and good expectation of Him. He did not know the road, so three roads presented themselves to him, and he took the middle one, and the pursuers came behind him and took the other two.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 23–24:

﴿When he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ he reached it; it was a well from which they used to draw water. ﴿He found upon it﴾ he found above its edge. ﴿A community of people﴾ a large group, of differing kinds. ﴿Watering﴾ their livestock. ﴿And he found, apart from them﴾ in a place lower than their place.

﴿Two women holding back﴾ restraining their sheep from the water, lest they mix with the sheep of the others. ﴿He said: "What is your affair?"﴾ what is your matter, that you hold back?

﴿They said: "We cannot water until the shepherds have driven off"﴾ until the shepherds turn their livestock away from the water, out of caution against mixing with the men. The object is omitted because the purpose is to show what indicates their chastity and prompts him to water for them, and then [he did so] behind it. Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read (yuṣdira) meaning "turn away" (yanṣarifa). It is also read al-ru'a' with a ḍammah, which is a collective noun like al-rukhal. ﴿And our father is an old man, very aged﴾ advanced in years, unable to go out to water, so he sends us out of necessity.

﴿So he watered for them﴾ their livestock, out of compassion for them. It is said that the shepherds used to place upon the mouth of the well a stone that only seven men or more could lift; he lifted it alone, despite his weariness, hunger, and the injury to his foot. It is also said that it was another well, over which there was a rock, and he lifted it and drew water from it. ﴿Then he turned back to the shade and said: "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need"﴾ for whatever reason You sent down to me.

﴿Of good﴾ little or much; most scholars understand it as food. ﴿In need﴾ poor, seeking. That is why it is construed with the preposition lām. It is also said that its meaning is: "Indeed, for whatever good of religion You sent down to me, I have become poor in this world, for he had been in plenty at the court of Pharaoh." The purpose of this is to express gratitude and thankfulness for that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 25–26:

﴿Then one of the two women came to him, walking bashfully.﴾ That is, modest and shy (mutakhaffiratan).

It is said that she was the younger of the two; and it is said she was the elder. Her name was Safurah, or Safra, and she is the one whom Musa (peace be upon him) married.

﴿She said: "Indeed my father invites you, so that he may reward you"﴾ — that he may recompense you.

﴿for having watered [the flock] for us.﴾ As a reward for your watering for us. ﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term and set out with his family﴾: with his wife. Perhaps I will bring you news from it"﴾: news of the road. Or a brand of thick wood, whether or not there was fire at its tip.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 32:

﴿Insert your hand into your bosom﴾, i.e., put it in. ﴿It will come out white, without harm﴾, i.e., without defect. ﴿And draw your arm close to you﴾, i.e., your two outstretched hands, with which you protect yourself from the serpent, like one who is frightened and startled, by placing the right hand under the left upper arm and vice versa. Or, by placing both of them into the bosom, which would be a repetition for another purpose, namely that doing so in the face of the enemy shows boldness and is a beginning of the manifestation of a miracle. It is also permissible that by "drawing close" is meant steadfastness and firmness when the staff turns into a serpent, used metaphorically from the condition of the bird: when it is afraid, it spreads its wings, and when it is safe and at ease, it folds them close to itself. ﴿From the fear﴾, i.e., on account of fear, meaning: when terror overtakes you, do this, showing fortitude and self-control. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read the ra' with a damma and the ha' with sukun (ar-rahb), and it is also read with a damma on both; Hafs read it with a fatha and sukun; all of these are dialectal variants (lughat). ﴿Those two﴾ is a reference to the staff and the hand, and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ruways read the dhal with tashdid (fa-dhannika). ﴿Two proofs﴾: two arguments (burhanan). Burhan is on the pattern fu'lan, from their saying abarra al-rajul, when he brought proof, from their saying barra al-rajul, when he became white; it is said barha' and barharahah for a white woman. It was also said that it is fa'lal, from their saying barhana. ﴿From your Lord﴾, sent with them. ﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾; indeed they were a people who were defiantly disobedient, so they were deserving of being sent to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 33–35:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I killed a person among them, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ (i.e., for it).

﴿And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent than me in tongue, so send him with me as a helper (ridan)﴾ meaning a supporter. Originally it is the name of that by which one is aided, like "difu'" (warmth). Nafi' read "ridan" with the light pronunciation (without the hamza and with the doubled letter lightened). ﴿who will confirm me﴾ by clarifying the truth, establishing the proof, and exposing the doubt. ﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾, for my tongue does not comply with me at the time of debate. It is said that the intended meaning is the people's confirmation of his (Harun's) explanation and clarification, but it was attributed to him by the attribution of the action to its cause. 'Asim and Hamzah read ﴿yusaddiqni﴾ with the nominative (raf'), on the basis that it is a description (sifah), and the response (jawab) is omitted.

﴿He said: "We will strengthen your arm through your brother"﴾ we will make you strong through him, for a person's strength lies in the strength of the hand for undertaking affairs, which is why it is expressed by the hand, and its strength by the strength of the upper arm (adud). ﴿And We will give you both authority﴾ dominance or proof. ﴿So they will not reach you﴾ by seizing or by argument. ﴿With Our signs﴾ is connected to something omitted, i.e., "go with Our signs"; or to "We will give" (najʿalu), i.e., "We will empower you by them"; or in the sense of "they will not reach," i.e., you will be protected from them; or it is an oath whose response is "they will not reach"; or it is an explanation of "the victorious" in His saying: ﴿You two and whoever follows you are the victorious﴾, in the sense that it is a complement to what it explains, or a complement to it on the basis that the lam in it is for definition and not in the sense of "alladhi" (who).(p-178)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 36–37:

﴿So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic."﴾ (It is) magic that you invent, the like of which has not been done before; or magic that you perform and then attribute to God; or magic that is described as fabrication, like all other kinds of magic. ﴿And we have not heard of this﴾ meaning the magic, or the claim of prophethood, ﴿among our forefathers of old﴾, existing in their times.

﴿And Moses said, "My Lord knows best who has come with the guidance from Him"﴾, so He knows that I am in the right and you are in the wrong. Ibn Kathir read "qala" (and he said) without the waw, because he (Moses) said what he said as a reply to their statement. The reason for the conjunction (with waw) is that the intent is to relate both statements, so that the observer may weigh them against each other and distinguish the sound from the corrupt. ﴿And whose will be the good outcome of the abode﴾: the praiseworthy outcome. The intended "abode" is this world, and its original outcome is Paradise, because it was created as a passage to the Hereafter; what is intended in it in essence is reward and punishment, and it is intended only incidentally.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (yakunu) with the ya' (yā’). ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾: they will not succeed in attaining guidance in this world and a good end in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 38–40:

﴿And Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself."﴾ He denied his knowledge of a god other than himself, not his existence, since he had nothing that required him to be certain of its non-existence. For this reason he ordered the building of the tower (al-sarh) so that he might climb up to it and look into the matter, by his saying: ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay and make for me a tower that I may look upon the god of Moses.﴾ It was as though he imagined that if there were such a god, it would be a body in the sky that could be reached by ascending. Then he said: ﴿And indeed, I think he is among the liars.﴾ Or he intended to build an observatory (rasad) from which he could observe the positions of the stars, to see whether among them there was anything indicating the sending of a messenger and the change of a dynasty. It has also been said that the meaning of the denial of knowledge is the denial of the thing known, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?﴾ Its meaning is "of what is not in them." This is one of the distinguishing features of practical (fi'liyyah) knowledge, since it necessarily entails the realization of its objects, so the absence of the objects entails the absence of the knowledge; this does not hold for receptive (infi'aliyyah) knowledge. It has been said that Pharaoh was the first to make bricks (al-ajurr) fired, and for this reason he ordered their making in a manner that includes teaching the craft, along with what it contains of self-aggrandizement. For this reason he called Haman by name with "ya" in the middle of speech.

﴿And he and his soldiers were arrogant in the land without right.﴾ Without entitlement. ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us.﴾ By resurrection.

Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (yurja'un) with a fatha on the ya and a kasra on the jim.

﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea.﴾ As its explanation has passed. In it is grandeur and magnification of the status of the One who seizes, and belittling of the two who are seized, as though He seized them all, despite their multitude, in one palm and cast them into the sea. Its parallel is: ﴿They did not appraise Allah with His true appraisal, while the earth entirely will be His grip on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand.﴾ ﴿Then observe,﴾ O Muhammad, ﴿how was the end of the wrongdoers,﴾ and warn your people against the like of it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 47:

﴿And had it not been that a calamity should afflict them for what their hands have sent forth, and they should say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?"﴾ The first *law* (*lawlā*, here the conditional particle of impossibility, *imtinā'iyyah*) and the second *law* (here the exhortative particle, *taḥḍīḍiyyah*) occurs within its context. The reason is that it is answered by *fa'* (the particle introducing the consequent) only as a figurative assimilation of it to the imperative. The verb *yaqūlū* (they say) is the object of the verb, and it is coordinated with *tuṣībuhum* (afflicts them) by *fa'*, which conveys the meaning of causation, drawing attention to the fact that speech is the intended purpose, in that it is the cause for the negation of what is answered by it, and that it would not proceed from them until punishment compels them. The answer is omitted, and the meaning is: "Had it not been for their saying, when a punishment afflicts them because of their disbelief and their sins, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger who conveys Your signs to us, so that we would follow them and be among the believers?'", *We did not send you*; that is, We sent you only to cut off their excuse and to establish the proof against them. ﴿So that we may follow Your signs﴾: meaning the messenger confirmed by a kind of miracle.

﴿And be among the believers﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 48–49:

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"﴾ That is, the entire Book, the hand, the staff, and other things, as a demand and an act of obstinacy. ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before?﴾ That is, the people of his kind in opinion and creed, who were the disbelievers of Musa's time. Or Pharaoh was an Arab, one of the descendants of ʿAd. ﴿They said, "Two sorceries"﴾ meaning Musa and Harun, or Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. ﴿backing each other up﴾ supporting one another by displaying those extraordinary acts, or by the agreement of the two Books. The Kufan readers recited «sihrān» with an elided noun (a genitive construction implied before it), or by making them "two sorcerers" for emphasis, or by ascribing their mutual support to their own action, indicating the cause of the inimitability (iʿjaz). «ẓāhiran» was also read, with idgham (assimilation of the consonants). ﴿And they said, "Indeed we are disbelievers in each of them."﴾ That is, in each of the two, or in all the prophets.

﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guided than both of them"﴾ than what was revealed to Musa and to Muhammad (ﷺ). Their pronoun is omitted because the meaning makes it clear. This supports that the intended "two sorcerers" are Musa and Muhammad. ﴿so that I may follow it, if you are truthful﴾ that we are two fabricated sorcerers. This is one of the conditional clauses meant to impose an obligation and rebuke them, and the particle of doubt is probably used sarcastically toward them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 52–53:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾. It was revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book. It is also said that it concerns forty men of the People of the Gospel: thirty-two who came with Ja'far from Abyssinia, and eight from Syria. The pronoun in "before it" (min qablihi) refers to the Qur'an, as does the implicit pronoun in:

﴿And when it is recited to them, they say: We believe in it﴾, meaning: that it is the Word of God Most High. ﴿Indeed it is the truth from our Lord﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what made them believe in it. ﴿Indeed we were Muslims before it﴾ is another resumptive clause (isti'naf) indicating that their belief in it is not something they newly invented at that time, but a matter whose time had long passed, since they saw its mention in the earlier Books, and since they were upon the religion of Islam before the Qur'an was revealed, or before it was recited to them, by their believing in its soundness in general terms.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 54–55:

﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾, once for their faith in their own Scripture and once for their faith in the Qur'an. ﴿Because they were patient﴾, with their patience and steadfastness in both faiths; or in faith in the Qur'an before and after its revelation; or in the harm inflicted by the polytheists and by those of their own religion who emigrated from them. ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾, meaning they repel disobedience with obedience, in accordance with his (ﷺ) saying: "Follow an evil deed with a good deed and it will erase it."

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ in the way of good.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 56–57:

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾: you are not able to bring them into Islam. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾: so He brings him into Islam. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾: of those who are prepared for that.

The majority of scholars hold that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, for when he was dying the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to him and said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah." He said: "O son of my brother, I know that you are truthful, but I dislike that it be said that he became afraid at death."

﴿And they say: If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land﴾: we will be driven out of it. It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Uthman ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf, who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "We know that you are upon the truth, but we fear that if we follow you and the Arabs oppose us, and we are 'akalat ra's (a people who devour one another's heads, i.e., a small, weak group), they will snatch us away from our land." Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary?﴾: Have We not made in their place a sanctuary secure, by the sanctity of the House in which the Arabs slaughter one another all around it while they themselves are safe within it? ﴿To which are brought﴾: are carried to it and gathered in it. Nafi' and Ya'qub, in one narration, read it with the letter ta' (tujba). ﴿The fruits of all things﴾: from every direction. ﴿As a provision from Us﴾: since this is their condition, though they are idolaters, how then would We expose them to fear and being snatched away when they combine the sanctity of the House with the sanctity of monotheism? ﴿But most of them do not know﴾: they are ignorant, not perceiving this nor reflecting so that they might know it. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying "from Us" (min ladunna), meaning: few of them reflect and thereby know that this is a provision from Allah, and most of them do not know, for if they knew they would not fear other than Him. The accusative of "provision" (rizqan) is either a verbal noun (masdar) from the sense of "is brought" (yujba), or a circumstantial state (hal) of "fruits," since it is made specific by its annexation. Then He clarified that the matter is the reverse, for they are more deserving of fearing the punishment of Allah in their current state, through His saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 58–59:

﴿And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood!﴾ That is, how many were the people of a town whose condition was like theirs in security and easy living, until they became insolent, so Allah destroyed them and ruined their dwellings. ﴿Those are their dwellings, not inhabited after them except a little.﴾ That is, they are desolate. ﴿Not inhabited after them except a little﴾ from habitation, since none dwells in them except passersby for a day or part of a day, or no one remains to dwell in them because of the evil consequences of their sins.

﴿And We were the inheritors﴾ of them, since no one succeeded them to dispose of their dwellings and all their affairs as they had disposed of them. The accusative of (مَعِيشَتَها) (maʿīshatahā, "their livelihood") is either by removing the preposition, or by making it an adverb of place in itself, as in your saying: Zayd ẓannī muqīm (Zayd is, in my opinion, residing), or by supposing a noun of time governed by it, or it is an object on the basis of making (بَطِرَتْ, baṭirat, "exulted") imply the sense of (كَفَرَتْ, kafarat, "was ungrateful").

﴿And your Lord was never one to destroy the towns﴾ and it was not His custom. ﴿until He had sent in their mother﴾ in its origin, which is its chief city, where its deeds are centered, because its people are more discerning and nobler. ﴿a messenger who recites to them Our verses﴾ to establish the proof and cut off excuse. ﴿And We never destroyed the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾ by denying the messengers and persisting in disbelief.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 60–61:

﴿And whatever you have been given is [merely] the enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment﴾ — from the means of this world. ﴿So it is the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment﴾ — you are provided for and adorn yourselves with it for the duration of your life, which is passing away. ﴿But what is with God﴾ — that is His reward ﴿is better﴾ in itself than that, because it is pure pleasure and complete delight. ﴿And more lasting﴾ because it is everlasting. ﴿Then will you not reason?﴾ — so that you would exchange what is lower for what is better. Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' (yaʿqilūn, "they reason"), and this is more forceful in admonition.

﴿Is one to whom We have promised a good promise﴾ — a promise of Paradise, for the goodness of a promise follows from the goodness of what is promised. ﴿and he is to meet it﴾ — will certainly attain it, since there is no failure in His promise; and for this reason He joined it with fa' (fa, "so"), which conveys the sense of causation. ﴿like one whom We have given enjoyment of the worldly life﴾ — which is mixed with pains, clouded with hardships, and followed by regret at its cessation. ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth﴾ — for reckoning or punishment. And "thumma" (then) indicates sequence in time or in rank. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, in one narration, and al-Kisa'i read "thumma hwa" with the ha' silent, likening the separate pronoun to the attached one. This verse is like a conclusion to the one before it, and for this reason it is connected to it with fa'.

**﴿وَيَوْمَ يُنادِيهِمْ﴾** ("And the Day He calls to them") is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) to "the Day of Resurrection," or it is in the accusative governed by the verb *udhkur* ("remember"). **﴿فَيَقُولُ أيْنَ شُرَكائِيَ الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾** ("So He will say: Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"). That is, "those whom you used to claim to be My partners." Both objects of the verb *tazʿumūn* have been omitted, because the context indicates them.

**﴿قالَ الَّذِينَ حَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ القَوْلُ﴾** ("Those against whom the Word has come true will say"): this is with the realisation of its requirement and the attainment of its consequence, which is His saying: **﴿لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنَ الجِنَّةِ والنّاسِ أجْمَعِينَ﴾** ("I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humankind, all together"), and other verses of warning. **﴿رَبَّنا هَؤُلاءِ الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾** ("Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray"). That is, "these are the ones whom we led astray," and the returning pronoun referring back to the relative clause has been omitted. **﴿أغْوَيْناهم كَما غَوَيْنا﴾** ("We led them astray as we ourselves went astray"): that is, "we led them astray, so they went astray with a deviation like our own deviation." This is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*, a new sentence beginning independently), indicating that they went astray by their own choice, and that they did nothing to them except whispering and enticement. It is also permissible for **﴿الَّذِينَ﴾** to be a qualifier (*ṣifah*, adjective), and **﴿أغْوَيْناهُمُ﴾** the predicate (*khabar*), on account of what is connected to it. Thus it adds something beyond the qualifier; and although it is a superfluous element (*faḍlah*), it has become one of the necessary parts.

That is, "they were not worshipping us; rather, they were worshipping their own desires." It has also been said that **﴿ما﴾** is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyyah*), connected to **﴿تَبَرَّأْنا﴾**, meaning: "We disown their worship of us."

"And it will be said, 'Call upon your partners.' So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, out of extreme bewilderment. [Lit. from the excess of bewilderment.] ﴿But they will not respond to them﴾ because of their inability to answer or to give help.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 76–78:

﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa﴾. He was his paternal cousin (ibn ʿammihi), Yashar ibn Qahith ibn Lawi, and he was among those who believed in him. ﴿So he transgressed against them﴾: he sought superiority over them and that they should be under his command, or he behaved arrogantly toward them, or he wronged them. It is said that this occurred when Pharaoh appointed him over the Children of Israel, or that he envied them, for it is narrated that he said to Musa, peace be upon him: "To you belongs the prophethood, and to Harun the high priesthood, while I have nothing; how long shall I endure this?" Musa said: "This is the doing of Allah."

﴿And We gave him of the treasures﴾: of the stored wealth. ﴿Indeed, its keys﴾: the keys of its chests, plural of miftah (with a kasra), which is that with which something is opened. It is said its treasuries; the regular singular is miftah. ﴿Were a burden to a band of strong men to bear﴾: the predicate of inna, and the clause is the relative clause of ma, and it is the second object of atay. Naa bihi al-himl means the load weighed him down until it bent him over; al-ʿusbah and al-ʿisabah mean a large group, and iʿsawsabu means they gathered together. It was also read as "la-yanuʾu" with the ya', treating the mudaf as taking the case of the mudaf ilayhi. ﴿When his people said to him﴾: it is in the accusative governed by "tanuʾu." ﴿Do not exult﴾: do not be insolent. Exultation in the world is blameworthy absolutely, because it is the result of loving it, being content with it, and being heedless of its passing away; for knowledge that what is in it of pleasure is bound to depart inevitably produces sorrow, as it has been said:

*The greatest grief for me in joy... is that its possessor is certain of its departure.*

For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾. Here He gave as the reason for the prohibition that it prevents the love of Allah the Exalted, so He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾, that is, those exultant over the adornments of the world.

﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you﴾ of wealth, ﴿the Hereafter abode﴾ by spending it on what makes it obligatory for you, for its purpose is that it be a means of reaching it. ﴿And do not forget﴾: and do not abandon, the abandonment of one who has forgotten, ﴿your share of the world﴾: which is that you obtain your Hereafter through it and take from it what suffices you. ﴿And do good﴾ to the servants of Allah ﴿as Allah has done good to you﴾ in what Allah has bestowed upon you. It is said: do good through thankfulness and obedience as He has done good to you by bestowing favors. ﴿And do not seek corruption in the earth﴾ by a matter that would be a cause of wronging and transgression; it is a prohibition against what he was upon of wronging and transgression. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ because of the evil of their deeds.

﴿He said: "I was given it only on knowledge I possess"﴾: I was preferred thereby over the people and deserved thereby to excel over them in rank and wealth. The phrase ʿala ʿilm is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it is the knowledge of the Torah, and he was the most knowledgeable of them in it. It is said it is alchemy; it is said it is the knowledge of trade, agriculture (dihqana), and all other means of earning; it is said it is knowledge of the treasures of Yusuf. ʿIndi is either an attribute of it or related to ʿutītuhu, as in your saying: "This is permissible in my view," that is, in my assumption and belief. ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations greater than him in strength and greater in accumulation?﴾ This is an expression of wonder and reproach at his being deceived by his strength and the abundance of his wealth, while he knew this, for he read it in the Torah and heard it from the memorizers of histories. Or it is a rejection of his claim to knowledge and his pride in it, by negating that knowledge from him: that is, does he possess such knowledge which he claims, yet did not know this, so that it would protect him from the fate of those who perished? ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾: a question of inquiry, for He, the Exalted, is aware of them; or a question of reproach, for they will be punished for them suddenly. It is as if, when He threatened Qarun by mentioning the destruction of those before him who were stronger and wealthier than him, He reinforced that by clarifying that He was not informed of their particular circumstances, but rather Allah is aware of the sins of all the criminals, and will certainly punish them for them.

Or it is a rejection of his claim to knowledge and his pride in it, by negating that knowledge from him: that is, does he possess such knowledge which he claims, yet did not know this, so that it would protect him from the fate of those who perished? ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾: a question of inquiry, for He, the Exalted, is aware of them; or a question of reproach, for they will be punished for them suddenly. It is as if, when He threatened Qarun by mentioning the destruction of those before him who were stronger and wealthier than him, He reinforced that by clarifying that He was not informed of their particular circumstances, but rather Allah is aware of the sins of all the criminals, and will certainly punish them for them.

﴿So he went out before his people in his finery.﴾ It is said that he went out on a white (shahba') mule, upon which was a crimson (al-urjuwan) saddle-cloth, and its saddle was of gold, and with him were four thousand men in his attire. ﴿Those who desired the life of this world said﴾ according to the common custom of people in their eagerness for it. ﴿"Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun was given!"﴾ They wished for something like it, not the same thing itself, out of caution against envy. ﴿"Indeed, he is possessed of great fortune."﴾ That is, of worldly fortune.

﴿But those who had been given knowledge said﴾ concerning the conditions of the Hereafter, to those who made the wish. ﴿"Woe to you!"﴾ This is an invocation of ruin (ihlak), used to rebuke what is not approved. ﴿"The reward of Allah"﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿"is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds"﴾ than what Qarun was given, indeed better than the world and everything in it.

﴿And it is not granted to﴾ the pronoun (al-damir) in it refers either to the statement that the scholars uttered, or to the word "reward" (thawab), since it carries the meaning of recompense (mathuba) or Paradise, or to faith and righteous deeds, since both of them carry the meaning of conduct (sira) and way (tariqa). ﴿except to those who are patient﴾ in obedience and in refraining from sins.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 81:

﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home.﴾ It is related that he used to harm Musa (peace be upon him) constantly, and Musa would bear with him out of kinship, until the zakat was revealed. So [Qarun] reconciled with him on the basis of one out of every thousand. He calculated it and found it too much, so he resolved to disgrace Musa among the Children of Israel so that they would reject him. He hired a prostitute (baghiyyah) so that she would accuse him by herself. Then, on the day of the festival, Musa stood up to preach and said: "Whoever steals, we shall cut off his hand; whoever commits fornication while unmarried, we shall flog him; and whoever commits fornication while married, we shall stone him." Qarun said, "Even if you were..." He said, "Even if I were." Qarun said, "The Children of Israel claim that you committed fornication with so-and-so." She was brought, and Musa (peace be upon him) adjured her by Allah to speak the truth. She said, "Qarun gave me a reward on condition that I accuse you by myself." Musa fell down weeping before his Lord, and Allah revealed to him: "Command the earth to do whatever you wish." So he said, "O earth, seize him!" and it seized him up to his knees. Then he said, "Seize him!" and it seized him up to his waist. Then he said, "Seize him!" and it seized him up to his neck. Then he said, "Seize him!" and he was swallowed up. Qarun kept pleading with him in these states, but he did not show him mercy. So Allah revealed to him: "How harsh you are! He asked you for mercy repeatedly and you did not show him mercy. By My might and My majesty, if he had called upon Me once, I would have answered him." Then the Children of Israel said, "He only did this so that he could inherit from him." So he called upon Allah, the Exalted, until the earth swallowed up his home and his wealth.

﴿So he had no company (fi'ah) to help him﴾ — fi'ah means helpers, derived from "fa'utu ra'sahu," meaning "I inclined his head" when I bent it. ﴿who could help him against Allah﴾ — by warding off His punishment from him. ﴿And he was not among those who could defend themselves (al-muntasirin)﴾ — those who could protect themselves from it, from their saying "nasarahu min 'aduwwihi, fa-ntasara," meaning he helped him against his enemy, so he was victorious, when he prevented him from him and he refrained.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 82–83:

﴿Those who had longed for his position the day before began to say﴾ — *manzilatahu* (his station). ﴿Yesterday﴾ — *bil-amsi*, meaning a short time ago. ﴿"Woe! It is as if Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants, and restricts it."﴾ — He extends and restricts according to His will, not because of a honour that requires extension, nor because of a humiliation that requires restriction. The word ﴿ويْكَأنَّ﴾ (*wayka'anna*), according to the Basran grammarians (*al-Basriyyun*, the grammarians of Basra), is compound: *way* (an exclamation of wonder) plus *ka'anna* (an expression of comparison), and the meaning is: "How alike the matter is: that Allah extends provision." It was also said that it derives from *wayka* in the sense of *waylaka* (woe to you), and *anna* is to be understood as if the sentence were *wayka i'lam anna Allaha* (woe to you, know that Allah...). ﴿Had Allah not been gracious to us﴾ — by not giving us what we wished for. ﴿He would have caused the earth to swallow us﴾ — because He had placed in us what He placed in him, so the earth swallowed us on account of it. Hafs read *lakhasafa* with a *fatha* on the *kha'* and the *sin*. ﴿"Woe! It is as if the disbelievers will not prosper."﴾ — for the blessing of Allah, or those who deny His messengers and what they were promised of the reward of the Hereafter.

﴿That abode of the Hereafter﴾ — a demonstrative of magnification, as if He said: "That which you have heard of and whose description has reached you." *Al-dar* (the abode) is a qualifier, and the predicate is: ﴿We shall make it for those who do not desire exaltation on the earth﴾ — domination and subjugation. ﴿Nor corruption﴾ — oppression of people, as Pharaoh and Qarun intended. ﴿And the good outcome﴾ — the praiseworthy one — ﴿is for the God-fearing﴾ — those who avoid what Allah does not approve.(p-187)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 84–85:

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is better than it﴾ in essence, measure and attribute. ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do﴾. He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, to express abhorrence of their state by repeating the attribution of evil deeds to them. ﴿Except what they used to do﴾, i.e., except the like of what they used to do; the "like" (mithl) was omitted and "what they used to do" was put in its place, for the sake of emphasizing the equivalence.

﴿Indeed, He who has imposed upon you the Qur'an﴾ made obligatory upon you its recitation, its conveyance, and acting by what is in it. ﴿Will surely return you to a place of return (ma'ad)﴾. Which ma'ad? It is either the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud) that He promised to raise you to therein, or Makkah, to which you longed to return; it is said that he returned to it on the day of the Conquest (al-fath). It is as if, when He decreed that ﴿the final outcome is for the righteous﴾ and confirmed that with the promise to the good-doers and the threat to the wrongdoers, He promised him the best outcome in both abodes.

It is narrated that when he reached al-Juhfah on his migration (hijrah), he longed for his birthplace and the birthplace of his forefathers, and so this was revealed. ﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance﴾ and what he deserves of reward and victory. The word "man" (who) is in the accusative, governed by a verb that the word "a'lam" (knows best) explains. ﴿And who is in manifest error﴾ and what he deserves of punishment and humiliation; by this he means himself and the polytheists. This is a confirmation of the earlier promise, and likewise His saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verses 86–87:

﴿And you did not hope that the Book would be cast down to you⁠﴾ meaning: He will return you to your place of return (ma'ad), just as He cast the Book down to you, though you had not hoped for it.

﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord⁠﴾ But He cast it down as a mercy from Him. It is also permissible that this be an exception (istithna') grammatically construed according to the meaning (mahmul 'ala al-ma'na), as if he had said: "The Book was not cast down to you except as a mercy."

﴿So do not be a supporter of the disbelievers⁠﴾ by flattering them (mudarat), bearing with them, and responding to their requests.

﴿And let them not turn you away from the signs of Allah⁠﴾ from reciting them and acting upon them. ﴿After they have been sent down to you⁠﴾ It is also read as "yaṣuddannaka" from aṣadda. ﴿And call to your Lord⁠﴾ to His worship and His oneness (tawhid). ﴿And do not be among the polytheists⁠﴾ by aiding them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 28, verse 88:

﴿And do not invoke with Allah another god.﴾ This and what precedes it are for stirring up (the believer's resolve) and cutting off the hopes of the polytheists of obtaining His assistance for them. ﴿There is no god but Him. Everything is perishing except His Face.﴾ Except His essence, for whatever else is other than Him is possible (mumkin) and perishing in itself, non-existent. ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾ the binding decree over creation. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ for recompense with truth.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Ta-Sin-Mim al-Qasas, he will have a reward equal to the number of those who believed in Musa and disbelieved, and there will not remain an angel in the heavens and the earth but that he will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection that he is truthful."
